item.title: Where does body fat go when we lose weight? The answer is stranger than you expect
item.description: Researchers estimate that around 84% of lost body fat is exhaled as carbon dioxide, while the remaining 16% is lost as water. Fuente: Euronews.

item.title: Resucitar el SR-71 Blackbird suena a locura. Cada vez más pistas apuntan a que la NASA se lo está planteando
item.description: Hace unos días, las redes echaron fuego después de que el administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, mostrase en una conferencia la silueta de lo que parecía el SR-71 Blackbird, uno de los aviones más emblemáticos de la NASA. Esta aeronave supersónica perteneció en primer lugar a la Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos. Sin embargo, después de trabajar en numerosas misiones de espionaje, pasó a manos de la agencia espacial, que lo usó como plataforma de investigación durante la década de 1990. Uno de los últimos Blackbirds que se usaron, el número 844, había permanecido expuesto desde entonces en el… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: 90-plus-day spaceflights linked to higher rates of hip fractures in astronauts
item.description: New research has found that the rate of hip fractures among astronauts after spaceflights lasting more than 90 days was higher than after shorter spaceflights or among people who were not astronauts. The findings of the study in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, underscore the need for expanded assessment of astronauts' long-term skeletal health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 1 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Harvest Moon with […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: ‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years
item.description: Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years, research has found, in a dramatic reshaping of the Alpine country whose big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say. Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Ajit Niranjan

item.title: Women astronauts use social media to reframe science and femininity together
item.description: Why can't a flight jacket be pink or purple? That was the question a 6-year-old girl asked her mother, Kellie Gerardi, an astronaut, researcher and science communicator. When Gerardi later appeared in a TV interview wearing a bright pink flight jacket, her daughter pointed to her mom on the TV screen, smiling with delight. This exchange—which appeared in a post on Gerardi's Instagram account—was a personal moment, skillfully presented through the language and visuals of social media. But it also conveys a clear message: Femininity and scientific credibility are not mutually exclusive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An Agricultural “Island” in the Saskatchewan River Delta
item.description: Surrounded by wetlands, Manitoba’s northernmost farmland near The Pas turns from green to brown over the 2026 growing season. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Wildlife tracking to fill gaps in monarch migration research
item.description: Every fall, monarch butterflies fuel up on nectar from Iowa's fall-blooming wildflowers before embarking on an extraordinary migration from North America to Mexico. But the pathways they take and how their travel is affected by weather and other factors have largely remained a mystery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hollywood se sacude: una jueza aprueba la histórica fusión de Warner Bros. Discovery con Paramount
item.description: Una jueza federal aprobó el miércoles 30 de septiembre un acuerdo que autoriza la adquisición de Warner Bros. Discovery por parte de Paramount, luego de que doce estados de EE. UU. impugnaran la operación. El acuerdo incluye garantías para la independencia editorial de 'CNN' y exige que el estudio resultante de la fusión estrene al menos 30 películas al año en sus dos primeros años. La compra ha sido rechazada por figuras de Hollywood que la consideran una amenaza a la industria. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: France 24

item.title: Philippines’ uranium find a ‘vital’ boost for nuclear energy ambitions
item.description: Researchers have identified a potential source of uranium in a long-explored mining district in the southern Philippines, as Manila moves to establish nuclear power and expand its critical minerals industry. The discovery, which could provide uranium for the nuclear fuel cycle if further exploration confirms its viability, was made in the Larap-Paracale mining district in Camarines Norte province, where exploration began in the 1950s. Researchers from the Philippine Nuclear Research Institute... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Sam Beltran

item.title: Christina Koch, astronauta de Artemis II y única mujer a bordo: “No hay nada que te prepare para la sensación de ver tu planeta iluminado”
item.description: Tras completar con éxito el histórico sobrevuelo lunar, se conoció una frase que la tripulante de la NASA pronunció mientras realizaba la misión Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Celebrity Traitors: Research suggests that some contestants will find the game tougher than it looks
item.description: "The Traitors" has become essential viewing for millions of fans. The TV game show, in which a group of "faithfuls" try to identify a smaller number of hidden traitors, is all about truth and lies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 100-million-year-old fossil reveals ancient outback bird
item.description: A chance and "extremely rare" discovery in an outback fossil pit has uncovered an unknown bird species from more than a hundred million years ago. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Tim Little and Susan Graham-Ryan

item.title: Fine-tuning cobalt for cleaner chemical transformations
item.description: Finding alternatives to precious metals in chemical manufacturing may be less like sourcing a substitute and more like tuning an instrument already in hand. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5016–5021: Fantastic Minerals and How To Detect Them
item.description: Written by Lucy Lim, Planetary Scientist at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Earth planning date: Friday, Sept. 18, 2026 Curiosity surprised us at the beginning of the week with a change in rock texture — instead of the finely layered bedrock blocks we’ve been seeing in our recent sulfate unit workspaces, suddenly we were looking […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Bacteria can make plant-based foods healthier for humans and animals
item.description: New research from the DTU National Food Institute and Aarhus University shows that microorganisms can be used to specifically alter the amino acid composition of plant-based foods, making them more nutritious and therefore healthier. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why some Ukrainian refugees struggle to rebuild their careers after arriving in Canada
item.description: The Russian invasion of Ukraine continues into 2026, with millions of Ukrainians displaced around the world. Many arrived in host countries with professional experience, degrees and specialized skills. Yet displacement often leaves highly educated refugees unable to continue their previous careers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists develop 'floating scarecrow' to protect threatened seabirds
item.description: New research has shown that a "floating scarecrow" developed by U.K.-based scientists and a repurposed bird-scaring kite can help save threatened seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Community-led archaeology project uncovers a major monastery of medieval Scotland
item.description: Community-led archaeology has uncovered the remains of an early medieval monastery in Argyll, western Scotland, identifying it as the high-ranking ecclesiastical center of Lios Mòr, previously known only from historical references and local traditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Devastating year for Switzerland's glaciers after extreme heat and low snow
item.description: Switzerland's glaciers lost more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026. Although melt rates did not quite reach the record levels of 2022, glacier thickness decreased by an average of 2.5 to 4 meters (8 to 13 feet) this year, and some glacier tongues lost up to 10 meters (33 feet) of ice. The research is published in the journal GLAMOS—Glacier Monitoring Switzerland. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Fuente: Radio Panamericana.

item.title: Confronting demons: How acoustic and AI technology brought ancient Etruscan tombs back to life
item.description: Although it is not always obvious, sound guides how we experience the world around us. And the latest archaeoacoustic techniques show that even the world's earliest architects understood this. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Key protein for cells' gene regulation needs a chaperone to do its job
item.description: A protein that's essential to every cell's ability to turn off unnecessary genes is well known for its key function of compacting genes and its connection to cancer when it undergoes mutation. But until now, scientists weren't quite sure how the protein gets where it needs to go to keep genes bound up so they aren't activated. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Peruvian mummies raise questions about Wari conquest of Nasca civilization
item.description: For centuries, historians have drawn the boundaries of where ancient people lived based on the evidence they left behind. By studying their remains, burial practices and other archaeological clues, they can determine the types of relationships they had with other people in the area. However, this can all change when new archaeological evidence is found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The real cost of coal mines to people and planet
item.description: The longer it takes to transition away from fossil fuels such as coal, the more costs accrue as climate change accelerates. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ocean predator chemical cues could provide early warnings for toxic algal blooms
item.description: A team of marine scientists led by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, has developed a new approach to predicting harmful algal blooms (HABs), changing how oceanographers track these hazardous marine events. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Catch a rare lunar occultation of Jupiter plus Saturn at opposition in early October
item.description: It's a busy skywatching month ahead. The first full week of October sees two top-notch skywatching events, with Saturn reaching opposition and the moon occulting Jupiter for North America on Oct. 6. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fluorescent sensors could help researchers see diabetes in action
item.description: Researchers from the University of Bath have developed fluorescent molecular probes that can detect changes in glucose levels inside living animals, giving scientists new ways of visualizing sugar uptake and studying diabetes, cancer and other metabolic diseases in whole organisms in real time. The findings are published in the journal Advanced Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Digging deep, researchers find high-altitude glacier endured last ice age
item.description: Ice cores recovered from an ice cap in northwestern Tibet appear to preserve fragments of ancient ice from the last ice age, extending Earth's glacial record by more than 100,000 years and making them the oldest ice cores ever recovered from the region, according to a new study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI scientist autonomously generates and validates new biological discoveries
item.description: Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have developed an AI scientist capable of generating scientific hypotheses, designing experiments and interpreting results. Making new biological discoveries with minimal human intervention is an important advance in self-driving laboratories. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Short on time? It could be good for you
item.description: When it comes to mental health, it may not be how much time you have that matters, but rather how you feel about the time you have. That's one key takeaway of a new University of Colorado Boulder study examining the relationship between time and mental health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tracking the fin whale and the sperm whale in the Mediterranean
item.description: Where are the great marine animals of the Mediterranean, such as the fin whale, the sperm whale or the bottlenose dolphin? How does their distribution change over a few weeks? All indications suggest that these species shift between marine areas in a remarkably short time and over relatively small spatial scales. Some species, such as the striped dolphin, maintain a relatively stable presence in certain areas, while others, such as the fin whale, move and concentrate in different areas from one observation campaign to the next. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anti-fibrotic drug could be repurposed to control cell communication
item.description: An experimental antifibrotic compound can dramatically alter how cells release the microscopic packages they use to communicate, according to new research from the University of Surrey. Researchers found that the compound, SD-208, which reduces scar tissue in organs, substantially reduced the release of extracellular vesicles, microscopic packages that cells use to carry proteins and other biological signals to neighboring and distant cells. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Help Overlap Zoo Reveal Cosmic Dust
item.description: Galaxies, vast collections of billions of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity, are scattered across the immensity of space. But every so often, a coincidence occurs: Two galaxies line up from our point of view on Earth (or from a space telescope) and appear to overlap in the sky. These rare overlapping galaxies […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA Adds New Science Investigations for Moon Base
item.description: Editor’s note: This release was updated on Sept. 30, 2026, to correct the name of the DISCO payload. NASA selected three new scientific investigations and their payload suites to advance our knowledge of the Moon and help pave the way for building humanity’s first lunar outpost, Moon Base. The suite of science instruments and technologies […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lauren E. Low

item.title: Scientists in 1960 predicted Friday 13 November 2026 will be 'Doomsday.' Should you be worried?
item.description: In 1960, Science, one of the world's leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. It predicted that on this future date—just over a month from today—the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 1 in 2 Florida residents live in HOAs—how these private governments are reshaping the American Dream
item.description: As she sat across from me drinking tea, Coretta—a pseudonym to protect her identity—shared her dismay about living in a central Florida community because of the control exercised by her homeowners association, or HOA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossil long known as world's oldest reptile dethroned
item.description: For nearly 30 years, a small fossil from Scotland has been celebrated as one of the earliest known reptiles. A new study out today in Nature and led by researchers at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, is rewriting that story. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Molecular movie' fills in blanks of how nonenveloped viruses infect cells
item.description: Viruses come in two major flavors—not chocolate and vanilla, quips Harvard Medical School structural biologist Stephen Harrison, but those enveloped in membranes, such as herpesvirus, influenza virus, HIV and SARS-CoV-2, and those that are not, such as poliovirus, HPV, rotavirus and adenovirus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Awards Contract to Develop 5G Communications for Moon
item.description: NASA has awarded Modulate Space Corporation a contract to develop key elements of a 5G communications system for use on the lunar surface with built-in Wi-Fi 6, for NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland. This accelerated effort is organized into two primary work areas that together will develop a scalable, standards-based communications capability designed to […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gerelle Q. Dodson

item.title: Clay tablets reveal how Babylonian students learned about their gods
item.description: When it came to religious education in ancient Babylonia, in what is now Iraq, students had a lot to learn, ranging from the names of gods to their divine characteristics. A new study published in the journal Iraq has taken a deep dive into ancient texts and surviving clay tablets to find out just how these traditions were taught in the classroom. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some threatened species may miss out as zoos try to balance conservation efforts with competing pressures
item.description: In the largest study of its kind, researchers at Nottingham Trent University analyzed more than 7,200 species across 613 zoos in 72 countries over a 30-year period. The team compared changes in zoo animal holdings with changes in species' conservation status, including extinction risk, international trade protections and involvement in zoo conservation breeding programs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mouse study reveals magnetic nanoparticles' potential for ectopic pregnancy diagnosis and treatment
item.description: A research team led by an Oregon State University scientist has demonstrated in a mouse model a potentially better way to care for women facing the life-threatening condition of ectopic pregnancy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wood beneath German lake may reveal buildings 3,000 years older than region's first farms
item.description: Underwater archaeological investigations have been taking place in Lake Arendsee (Altmarkkreis Salzwedel) for several years. The discovery of Neolithic fish weirs, a high medieval barge (flat-bottomed cargo ship) and a late medieval dugout canoe attracted considerable attention. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Groups of genetically identical fish follow different behavioral paths as they mature
item.description: Schooling fish have long fascinated us with their mesmerizing collective movements and seemingly perfect coordination. But a new study on clonal mollies suggests that this behavior is not innate. During their first days of life, the fish still display distinct individual behaviors, and it is only around one month of age that they begin to form cohesive shoals, developing the coordinated movements characteristic of the group. However, several shoals of genetically identical clones begin to behave differently after a few weeks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UV light locks radiation-detecting materials into durable, water-resistant films
item.description: Florida State University researchers have developed a method to make a class of materials more robust and potentially easier to manufacture for advanced radiation detection devices, including those used in medical imaging and radiation therapy as well as space technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: The new BMW 3 Series shows just how quickly EVs have caught up to fossil fuel vehicles on pricing. Fuente: TechCrunch.

item.description: Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: AI-enhanced petitions on Change.org: More text, less success
item.description: The change was obvious—but in the end, things stayed about the same. Cornell researchers took advantage of online petition website Change.org's gradual rollout of an artificial intelligence writing tool to gauge AI-enhanced language's impact on petition outcomes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New click beetle species named after Dominican Republic's Indigenous Arawak people
item.description: A new species of click beetle with a glossy and highly domed black body has been described from cloud forest sites in the mountains of the Dominican Republic and named in honor of the Arawak peoples who lived on the island before European colonization. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Research collaboration helps Gulf Coast communities plan for the unpredictable
item.description: For communities along the Gulf Coast, hurricane season presents a recurring challenge: knowing when, where and how to evacuate before a major storm hits. To tackle this, researchers at Texas A&M University have spent more than a decade helping local, state and federal agencies develop clear, data-driven evacuation strategies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mysterious oarfish's fins inspire large underwater robot design
item.description: When designing a large underwater robot that could swim silently to avoid startling sea creatures, roboticist Rob Shepherd considered the unusual swimming system of oarfish, the meters-long fish whose ribbon-like dorsal fin moves in waves to propel its body. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How sea squirts perceive underwater noise
item.description: Shipping, construction work and other human activities are altering the acoustic conditions in our planet's seas. Sound pressure is often examined to determine the effects that this underwater noise has on marine organisms. However, these observations may not be thorough enough for creatures that live on the seafloor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: International study identifies key childhood experiences that predict happiness and well-being in adulthood
item.description: A new study, led by the University of Nottingham and conducted across three countries, has identified a set of key childhood experiences that predict multiple measures of well-being in adulthood—including health, happiness, anxiety, life satisfaction, satisfaction with social relationships and general trust in others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA, International Partners Advance Work on Space Crops
item.description: NASA, CSA (Canadian Space Agency), and the German Aerospace Center signed a joint statement of intent to begin coordinated, preparatory work toward an Earth-based demonstrator to learn how to grow crops on the Moon. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Women leave psychology research more often than men, especially early in their careers
item.description: Today, women are more likely than men to begin an academic career in psychology. Nevertheless, they leave research substantially more often, particularly during the first years after entering the field. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chlamydia packs DNA with lipids, revealing possible target for blocking infection
item.description: The bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis is one of the most common causes of sexually transmitted infections worldwide. Biologically, it is regarded as a highly specialized "nutrient thief": Because chlamydia have lost the ability to reproduce independently outside a host cell, they hijack human metabolic products—particularly sphingolipids—for their own development. Within the host cell, they create a sheltered environment known as an inclusion. These bacterial colonies often grow so large that they exceed the size of the human host cell's nucleus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Poverty in the EU declined in the last decade, but disparities persist among nations
item.description: Despite differences among nations, poverty in the European Union declined between 2015 and 2023, according to a study published in PLOS One by Silvia Megyesiova and Cecilia Olexova of the Bratislava University of Economics and Business in Košice, Slovak Republic. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Adult fossil strengthens evidence for Homo erectus in southern Africa 2 million years ago
item.description: La Trobe archaeologists have described 18 new hominin fossils, including a second Homo erectus skull fragment that confirms the species first appeared in southern Africa 2.0 million years ago—200,000 years earlier than traditionally thought. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3D light fields push electrons into quantum states previously beyond experimental reach
item.description: By superimposing two ultrashort laser pulses that converge from different directions, a team of physicists at the University of Oldenburg has succeeded in generating three-dimensional light fields. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Criminal conspiracy to steal used cooking oil shows how trash can become treasure
item.description: Federal prosecutors recently described an interstate criminal enterprise with all the trappings of organized crime: clandestine warehouses, money laundering and stolen goods transported across state lines. The mid-September 2026 announcement stated that 19 defendants faced charges; two had just pleaded guilty, while the remainder are slated for trial in April 2027. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Zinc oxide quantum dots enable faster charge detection, laying groundwork for spin qubits
item.description: Researchers at Tohoku University, in collaboration with the National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS) and the University of Tokyo, have taken an important step toward semiconductor quantum computing using zinc oxide (ZnO). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Honeybee silk could power smarter wound dressings
item.description: Biodegradable films made from engineered honeybee silk could form the basis of a new generation of "smart" wound dressings, according to researchers at CSIRO and Adelaide University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hidden star cluster discovered in Milky Way's crowded disk defies easy classification
item.description: Astronomers have discovered a stellar cluster hidden in the crowded disk of the Milky Way. The object, named Garro 04, was first identified as an unusual collection of stars in observations from the VVVX survey and was later confirmed using infrared spectroscopy. A paper outlining the properties of this seemingly mysterious stellar system was posted to the arXiv preprint server on September 21. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn't replace speaking with an actual person
item.description: Approximately 30% of U.S. adults who were learning a language in 2025 reported that they were using artificial intelligence as a resource. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sugar found in meteorites may have helped secure its own survival on early Earth
item.description: Is there life elsewhere, or is Earth unique in the universe? This is one of humanity's great unanswered questions. One way to approach this mystery is to investigate how life began here on Earth. Our research explores the conditions in which a mixture of molecules somehow transformed from chemistry into biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stoicism isn't just for men—despite what the manosphere suggests
item.description: Stoicism has attracted all sorts of fans in recent years, but one group whose interest in this ancient philosophy has attracted a good deal of comment is the "manosphere." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dark kitchens are popping up everywhere, but what are they and why does it matter?
item.description: When you order food through an app, how much do you know about where you're buying it from? It could be a restaurant on the local main street or one located in a warehouse in a faraway industrial park. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth and Mars: Built from different cosmic recipes
item.description: Four and a half billion years ago, Earth and Mars were born in the rotating cloud of gas and dust that would eventually become our solar system. Yet exactly how the planets formed remains one of the most disputed questions in planetary science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cities across the world are sinking because of groundwater depletion, but the process can be reversed
item.description: Many cities around the world are sinking because too much water is extracted from the groundwater reservoirs beneath them. This sinking makes these coastal cities more exposed to rising seas as the climate warms. But as our new research shows, this process can work in reverse: When groundwater is replenished, cities can rise. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Alpine bacteria show unexpected ability to fight viruses
item.description: A silent, long-running competition has been taking place in Swiss alpine lakes for millions of years, killing trillions of organisms every day without anyone noticing. This competition between bacteria and viruses pushes both into a relentless evolutionary battle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Drones, satellites and AI help scientists watch over Antarctica's smallest lifeforms
item.description: Monitoring Antarctica's tiny, scattered ecosystems is a challenge that has long plagued researchers. But a new study led by the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new approach to tracking life in one of the most remote environments on Earth. The research is published in the ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: The safety and sterilization of pharmaceuticals manufacturing
item.description: Manufacturing modern medicines is a multistage process, and each step introduces the opportunity for contamination, which can be both deadly and expensive. Recently, epinephrine injections, used for severe allergic reactions, were recalled due to a lack of assurance of sterility, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-activated crystals break down DNA-like molecules in water, potentially curbing antibiotic resistance
item.description: Engineers have developed a new approach for turning ordinary water into a weapon against antibiotic-resistant bacteria, according to a study published in the journal Chem Catalysis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Butterflies use optical illusions to dodge predators
item.description: A bird attacking a butterfly will often find its beak snapping at thin air. According to new research, that split-second miss isn't just bad luck. It's caused by a visual illusion from the butterfly's wings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Asgard archaea suggest crawling motility may be far older than previously thought
item.description: Asgard archaea, our closest known microbial relatives, play a key role in current models of the origin of more complex organisms, known as eukaryotes (all animals, plants, protists and fungi). However, their biology has so far been poorly understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study reveals how tilapia adapt to extreme salt stress
item.description: In the world of aquatic life, the Mozambique tilapia (Oreochromis mossambicus) is remarkably tolerant of saltwater, surviving in habitats ranging from fresh water to hypersaline ponds three times saltier than the ocean. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As I said… How intonation influences perception
item.description: "Between the lines"—that's how we describe unspoken messages that the actual text may omit but that are conveyed, for example, through word choice or tone of voice. A research team led by the Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics (MPIEA) in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, has investigated how we convey meaning through speech intonation and identified different listener profiles. The results have been published in Cognition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
item.description: Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival. The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent

item.title: Laser-made muons produce first images of dense objects
item.description: Muons are constantly being created as cosmic rays collide with molecules in Earth's upper atmosphere. With their ability to penetrate far into dense, solid materials, these cosmic muons are often used to image the insides of objects that are otherwise hidden from view. However, the flow of these natural particles is far too slow for the technique to become both fast and reliable in practical settings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unlocking the cell's supply chain: How cholesterol keeps cellular recycling centers running
item.description: Mention cholesterol, and most people will think of clogged arteries or health warnings. But inside the microscopic universe of the human cell, cholesterol has a drastically different job description as an indispensable cellular lifesaver. A study led by the Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine (LKCMedicine) at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore), shows how cells rapidly dispatch cholesterol to reinforce their "recycling centers" called lysosomes, preventing them from bursting while breaking down worn-out cellular machinery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research
item.description: Security service says academics should stop taking grants from and working with firm backed by China’s intelligence service MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities China’s intelligence service used a front company to pay grants to British universities and steal crucial research about technology projects, MI5 said on Wednesday in a rare public espionage warning. Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

item.title: The north pole of Mars is less dusty than scientists thought
item.description: Although Mars may have once resembled Earth, the rocky red planet now appears far from hospitable. Still, certain details—such as ice-bound water—pique researchers' curiosity. As on Earth, ice on Mars contains valuable records of past climate that could reveal whether the planet hosts, or has ever hosted, life. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Starship's first orbital flight put its heat shield to the test
item.description: SpaceX's Starship, the most powerful launch vehicle ever developed, reached Earth orbit for the first time on Sept. 28, 2026. This mission, the rocket's 14th test flight, also marked the first time that Starship deployed Starlink internet satellites into the existing larger constellation: 26 new next-generation nodes in total. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cannabis users were twice as likely to commit violence, review finds
item.description: A review of more than 265,000 people found that cannabis use was associated with higher rates of both committing violence and becoming a victim of it. The researchers say the link is significant but does not prove cannabis itself is the cause. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: More cats: The key to happy countries?
item.description: National happiness is influenced by complex relationships beyond basic economic factors, according to a study by Javier I. Borráz-León of the Secretariat of Science, Humanities, Technology, and Innovation in Mexico City and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A record-breaking X-ray flash may reveal the birth of a magnetar
item.description: Astronomers have found strong evidence that some mysterious, minutes-long X-ray flashes are produced when two neutron stars collide and create a magnetar. One record-setting event glowed in X-rays for nearly 10 minutes, potentially opening a new way to find these extreme cosmic mergers. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Co-design with the community? Study provides insights on building trust
item.description: Co-design projects give stakeholders a seat at the table, including them as members of the design team, but few studies have evaluated whether they feel heard. A participant satisfaction study found that how and when people are engaged, as well as who holds decision-making power, shape meaningful participation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ocean heatwaves are hiding months of extra warming
item.description: Marine heatwaves may be only the most intense part of much longer warming events, with elevated temperatures sometimes lingering for months. Researchers found that conventional measurements underestimate total heat exposure by more than 150% on average, potentially overlooking a major source of stress on marine ecosystems. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: E. coli survives longer in poultry-amended Georgia onion soils, two-year study finds
item.description: New research suggests that poultry litter-based soil amendments and weather conditions, particularly extreme weather events, may influence how long bacteria survive in agricultural soils used to grow sweet onions. The findings could help inform food safety risk management for produce growers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New simulations connect the first stars to cosmic fingerprints still visible today
item.description: Researchers have used some of the most detailed simulations yet of the early universe to investigate how the first stars and galaxies formed. Led by researchers at the University of Bath in the U.K., alongside collaborators at the University of Chicago in the U.S. and the Institut d'Astrophysique de Paris in France, the MEGATRON project uses advanced simulations to explore how the first stars and galaxies lit up the previously dark cosmos and enriched it with the chemical elements that would later become the building blocks of everything around us. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UK banks are Europe’s biggest coal financiers, report finds
item.description: Study says UK-based banks provided $8.3bn in coal financing in four years, with Barclays and HSBC leading rise UK banks are Europe’s biggest financial backers of the global coal industry, providing billions of pounds in funding for the climate-wrecking fossil fuel in the past four years, according to a report. The study found UK-based banks had provided $8.3bn (£6.2bn) in coal financing since Cop26 in Glasgow in 2021 , when global leaders pledged to “phase down” coal use. This compared with $4.9bn from German banks and $3.4bn from French banks over the same period. Continue reading... Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Taylor

item.title: Mulberry may reshape gut bacteria and influence metabolism
item.description: Mulberry compounds may reshape the gut microbiome in ways that support intestinal health and metabolism, with some combinations showing especially strong effects in animal studies. However, the results vary depending on the plant part and processing method, and the benefits have yet to be confirmed in humans. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: After 20 years, jet diffusion wakes detected in quark-gluon plasmas
item.description: Boats passing over smooth water form a pair of diffusion wakes behind them veering off at a certain angle. Turbulence occurs along the line directly behind the boat, but the two diffusion waves are at a theoretical angle of 19.5° from the same line, for deep, ideally smooth water. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Who decides what time it is? The politics behind contested clocks
item.description: Despite contentious local debates about time zones and seasonal shifts, University of Queensland research shows there is no official global time zone system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
item.description: NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Gene-silencing technology to protect forests from invasive pests
item.description: A University of Kentucky forest entomologist is advancing a pest-control approach designed to target destructive forest beetles while minimizing effects on surrounding wildlife. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Los astronautas pasan mucho tiempo estreñidos, ahora sabemos que todo está relacionado con un problema más grave
item.description: Los viajes espaciales pueden tener muchos efectos sobre la salud de los astronautas . Hoy en día sabemos que afectan a los huesos, los ojos, el corazón y hasta los riñones , entre otros órganos y sistemas. También sabemos que los astronautas suelen tener bastantes problemas para ir al baño. No es raro, ya que la microgravedad ralentiza el descenso de los alimentos por el intestino. El problema es que el estreñimiento no es el único efecto de esa ralentización digestiva. Ahora, un nuevo estudio apunta a que hay otras consecuencias mucho más perjudiciales. La parte positiva es que conocerlas es… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Wild crabapples have genetic potential to improve domestic varieties
item.description: A bad apple doesn't always ruin the bunch. In fact, it might make the bunch a little stronger. A new study published in Horticulture Research by Ben Mansfeld, an assistant professor of biology in Arts & Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis, provides apple breeders with a genomic resource to help harness the power of humble crabapples. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Engineered nanostructured surfaces could offer a new way to limit marine biofouling
item.description: Researchers at Sultan Qaboos University have developed engineered surfaces that combine microscopic patterns with zinc oxide nanorods to reduce the attachment of bacteria and microalgae—a process that contributes to biofouling on submerged marine and industrial equipment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
item.description: Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge, leaving a glowing trail hundreds of thousands of light-years long. By keeping this gas hot and preventing it from falling inward, the jets may help determine whether a galaxy keeps forming stars or becomes quiet. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Chinese researchers say missile lidar model can spot US F-35 at up to 61.5km
item.description: A computer simulation developed by Chinese researchers suggests that a missile-borne system with the latest light detection and ranging system, or lidar, could detect and track an F-35 stealth fighter at up to 61.5km (38 miles) at night. The theoretical model developed by a leading Chinese air force missile supplier says that under ideal conditions, the claimed range could have implications for the F-35’s ability to survive while facing China’s stealth fighters. But one analyst is sceptical that... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Chao Kong

item.title: Snakes' appearances linked to how scary or appealing people find them
item.description: Snakes can elicit a wide range of human responses, including fear, disgust, awe and admiration. Past studies suggest that both humans and nonhuman primates, such as monkeys and apes, tend to quickly notice snakes in their surroundings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pompeii’s 2,000-year-old eruption just gave scientists a better clock for Earth’s past
item.description: Mount Vesuvius’ famous 79 CE eruption has given scientists a remarkably precise benchmark for dating events deep in Earth’s past. The improved technique could sharpen the timelines of volcanic eruptions, asteroid impacts, extinctions, and other major moments in geological history. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
item.description: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along. Fuente: Deutsche Welle - World.

item.title: 4-winged fossil found in Liaoning challenges single origin of dinosaur flight
item.description: Scientists have unveiled an exceptionally well-preserved 100-million-year-old fossil of a small, feathered dinosaur in northeastern China that could reshape our understanding of how dinosaurs took to the skies. The newly discovered species, named Norellraptor barsboldi, is a four-winged predatory dinosaur measuring 57cm (22 inches) long. Belonging to the microraptorines – small dinosaurs with feathers and wings closely related to birds – the creature offers fresh evidence that flight evolved... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Holly Chik

item.title: Watch Live: NASA’s Crew-13 could make the fastest U.S. trip to the ISS ever
item.description: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission is scheduled to launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1. The Dragon could reach the orbiting laboratory in just 7 hours and 50 minutes, making it the fastest U.S. spacecraft journey to the ISS in history. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Science begins for Smile
item.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: David Lulasa ha comentado: How in the first place?
item.description: The Maldives' coral reefs are among the most biodiverse in the Indian Ocean. To understand and better protect these reefs, marine biologists are... Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Paw-fect candidate: Australia finds new koala rescue dog
item.description: The hunt is over: After trawling through dozens of applications, an Australian animal welfare group has found a successor to a hero hound credited with saving more than 100 koalas from fires. Fuente: Phys.org.
